stories.headline: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
stories.script: Our lead story today. OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over a breach of Medicare data in Australia, but Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has signalled changes to criminal law aimed at future breaches by artificial intelligence companies, the Guardian reports. The government says the changes are meant to stop firms from claiming in future that they were unaware a computer was loaded. On Tuesday, Albanese published the recommendations of a rapid review into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting portal run by Services Australia. He did not release the review's findings or the full report, but committed to doing so at a later date. Among the measures outlined is keeping security controls in place throughout every stage of development and deployment.

stories.headline: Mandatory AI safety and security protections announced after OpenAI breach of Medicare video
stories.script: Also today. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said his government will establish a new regulator for AI safety, according to the Guardian. He added that Labor would weigh six key obligations for artificial intelligence companies. The announcement follows the breach of Medicare involving OpenAI. Albanese said, "We accept all of the recommendations," adding that implementation work has begun.

stories.headline: Ant Group’s Robbyant open-sources tactile AI model for robot hands
stories.script: In China. Robbyant, the robotics arm of Ant Group, has made the model weights and inference code for LingBot-Touch publicly available, TechNode reports. The model is built to help robot hands use touch when handling objects. It was trained on almost 5,000 hours of recordings from three kinds of touch sensors, so it can operate across different hardware. Robbyant tested it on 26 real-world tasks with two robotic hands, including handling fragile items and coordinating both hands.

stories.headline: Qantas to cut 850 Australian jobs and outsource work to India under AI-driven overhaul
stories.script: Turning to India. Qantas plans to eliminate 850 jobs in Australia and move work offshore as part of an overhaul driven by artificial intelligence, the Guardian reports. The airline announced a deal with Accenture, with chief executive Vanessa Hudson pointing to unprecedented technological disruption. It is the third large layoff plan unveiled by an Australian company in three weeks, following restructuring announced by design firm Canva and National Australia Bank.

stories.headline: Teenager who planned terror attack in Sydney tells court he was radicalised online and used AI to strategise
stories.script: Around the world. A 16-year-old who admitted planning a terrorist attack in Sydney in 2024 has told a court that his radicalisation began online, the Guardian reports. The boy, identified only as RK because of his age, said he first came across extremist content on TikTok. He then moved to Telegram and YouTube to find instructions for making bombs, and used ChatGPT to work out his plans. RK pleaded guilty to acts in preparation for, or planning, a terrorist act. In a sentencing decision delivered on Monday, the New South Wales supreme court spared him a prison term. Instead, the court placed him on a three-year community corrections order.

stories.headline: The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes
stories.script: Next. A hack that caused fridges in France to defrost has been blamed on Iran, and is presumed to be connected to similar incidents elsewhere in Europe, according to the Guardian. The attack has been described as not particularly complex. Iranian hackers have a record of using their intrusions to make a point. In 2023, a state-backed group disrupted television streaming in the United Arab Emirates to air a deepfake report about the war in Gaza. That same year, Iran-linked hackers put the slogan down with Israel on screens of water-control equipment built by an Israeli company.

stories.headline: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
stories.script: From the research desk. Robots that handle objects with their hands depend heavily on a sense of touch, but today's commercial touch sensors are still immature, and each type has its own strengths and weaknesses. In a paper titled Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation, the researchers present LingBot-Touch, a large foundation model for touch. It produces a single shared representation from pressure-based, magnetic and camera-based touch sensors, and can be extended to new sensor types. Its output plugs directly into different robot control systems, including vision-language-action models. Tests in simulation and on several real robots showed it substantially improved complex handling tasks while remaining computationally efficient.
